newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Inflation slowdown surprises Philippine economists.
newsitem.headline: Inflation slowdown surprises Philippine economists.

text.p: A modest slowdown in Philippine inflation surprised many economists on Monday who were expecting a slight acceleration following a series of oil price increases.

"This is better than expected," Al Rillo, an economist at DBS Securities, said after the National Statistics Office announced prices rose a year-on-year 4.6 percent in April, down from 4.8 percent in March.
"I was thinking that the oil price adjustment would have some impact on commodity prices ... Apparently it did not," Rillo said.
The food, beverage and tobacco index, which comprises the biggest group in the inflation basket, slipped to 1.8 percent from 1.9 percent in March.
Inflation in food alone dipped to 1.6 percent from 1.7 percent in March.
A recent Reuter poll of six analysts showed that they were projecting an average rise of 4.98 percent due to the higher fuel prices.
"It's a welcome surprise. The market is getting quite excited about the number," Fiona Paua, research head of Citicorp Securities, said.
The Philippine stock composite index, which was severely battered in the past weeks, recovered strongly by midsession, gaining 2.56 percent to 2,672.30.
Luz Lorenzo, the chief economist of Peregrine Securities, said the slowdown was likely to prompt many economists to revise their inflation target for the whole year.
Many were close to the government's own targetted range of six to seven percent.
But Lorenzo said she might lower her full-year target of 5.9 percent which is already lower than the consensus.
"I'm quite sanguine about the inflation rate ... I don't think inflation will go up significantly in the coming months," she said.
However, Rillo said prices on food products might still go up in the coming months due to tighter supply.
"Right now, we are not inclined to change our full-year target of seven percent ... We might still see some price upticks in the second semester, especially in rice and corn," he said.
But Paua said any supply shortage during the lean months of the agriculture sector could be easily filled up through importation.
She also doused fears that a heightened spending pattern might emerge in the latter part of the year, as politicians start releasing money in preparation for next year's general elections.
"The Central Bank is very much equipped to deal with this type of situation. I think that will be manageable," Paua added.
On Sunday, the Central Bank reported that it was able to keep a tight rein on money supply growth. Growth in the base and reserve money levels were kept at only 10 percent in April.
